Service guide

Home battery installation

Storage is a sizing decision, not a shopping decision.

Request an assessmentAll services

A battery only earns its place when it is sized against your evening load, your solar surplus and your tariff. An oversized battery is an expensive unused asset; an undersized one leaves savings on the table.

We model how much of your generation is currently exported at a low feed-in rate, how much of that could be shifted into your own evening consumption, and what a particular battery size is realistically worth for your household.

A home battery is a set of specifications wearing a marketing department. This guide walks through the numbers that actually determine what a battery can do for a household — capacity, power, efficiency, chemistry and lifespan — and the honest test of whether one is worth buying in your situation.

Capacity is not power — the two numbers that get confused

Capacity, measured in kilowatt hours (kWh), is how much energy the battery can store. Power, measured in kilowatts (kW), is how much it can deliver at any instant. A battery is sized in kWh but limited by kW; both figures decide whether it can do a given job.

A battery with generous capacity but modest power output may cover a whole evening of gentle household loads but struggle to run an oven, hot water system and air-conditioner together. A high-power battery with small capacity will happily run those appliances — briefly, before it is flat.

Illustration of the arithmetic on a battery rated at 10 kWh / 5 kW — figures illustrate the maths, not any specific product
SpecificationIllustrative valueWhat it means in practice
Nameplate capacity10 kWhThe headline number on the brochure
Usable capacity at 90% depth of discharge9 kWhWhat the battery management system will actually let you draw
Continuous power5 kWThe largest load it can run steadily — about one large appliance at a time
Peak power (short bursts)7–8 kW, often time-limitedEnough to start a motor or compressor briefly, such as a fridge or pump
Round-trip efficiency (say 90%)≈ 8.1 kWh returnedEnergy delivered to the house for the 9 kWh discharged

Round-trip efficiency, and why it matters to your bill

Every time energy passes through a battery, some of it is lost — in conversion, in chemistry, in heat. Round-trip efficiency measures what comes back out compared with what went in; for modern home systems it is commonly in the order of 85–95% once conversion losses are counted.

That loss is why storage value depends on the gap between what you are paid for exports and what you pay for imports. Storing a kilowatt hour you could have sold for a few cents, in order to avoid buying one at many times that price, is the trade a battery is making. If the gap is small, so is the gain.

Battery chemistry, at a high level

Most new stationary home batteries use lithium iron phosphate (LFP) cells, which are prized for long cycle life and good thermal stability. Some products use nickel manganese cobalt (NMC) chemistry, which stores more energy per kilogram and per litre — useful where space is tight. Both chemistries are proven in home storage; the difference shows up in cost, footprint, cycle life and how the manufacturer warranties throughput.

Whatever the chemistry, the visible behaviour is governed by the battery management system (BMS): the electronics that monitor cell voltage and temperature, balance the cells, enforce depth-of-discharge limits and protect the pack from conditions that shorten its life.

A normal day in the life of a battery

  1. Early morning: the house runs from the grid, or from leftover stored energy if the battery is programmed to support that.
  2. Morning to midday: solar generation first serves the house; surplus charges the battery.
  3. Afternoon: once the battery is full, further surplus is exported — or, under some tariffs, held back by export limits.
  4. Evening peak: the battery discharges to cover household loads, which is where most of the financial value is created.
  5. Overnight: the battery may continue to supply gentle loads, or hold capacity; the rest comes from the grid.

On some tariffs and in some jurisdictions, batteries can also be programmed to charge from the grid at cheap times — usually overnight — and discharge during expensive periods. Whether that is permitted and profitable depends on local rules and the price spread; it should be discussed honestly rather than assumed.

Backup capability — what a battery can and cannot do

During a blackout, a grid-connected solar system must switch off unless it has battery storage and correct backup wiring. Anti-islanding protection exists to keep network lines safe for the people repairing them; a battery with backup capability sidesteps the problem by supplying your home from a stored reserve.

  • A dedicated backup circuit runs only selected circuits — usually lights, fridge, internet and a few power points. This is the most common and most affordable configuration.
  • Whole-home backup needs equipment and battery power sized to your largest loads' starting surge, not just their running watts.
  • Motors and compressors — air-conditioners, pumps, fridges — draw a brief surge well above their rated power when starting. A battery's peak rating is what handles that.

Decide backup before installation, not after

Which circuits are backed up is a wiring decision made on installation day. Changing your mind later means re-opening the switchboard. If outage protection matters — for medical equipment, working from home, or just peace of mind — say so at design time.

What determines a battery's lifespan

  • Temperature — a battery in a hot garage or direct western sun ages faster than the same battery in a shaded, ventilated position. Placement is a design decision, not an installation detail.
  • Cycles and depth — regular deep cycling wears cells more than shallow cycling; the BMS manages this, but usage patterns still matter.
  • State of charge extremes — batteries last longer when they spend less time pinned at 0% or 100%.
  • Throughput — manufacturers typically warrant a total energy throughput (measured in megawatt hours) as well as a calendar period. A heavily cycled battery can reach its throughput limit before its calendar warranty ends.

When a battery is likely to pay off — and when it is not

  • Strong case: a large solar surplus exported at a low feed-in rate, high evening consumption, and a wide gap between import and export prices.
  • Strong case: evening-dominated usage with time-of-use pricing, where stored energy displaces the most expensive hours.
  • Weaker case: a household that already self-consumes most of its generation because someone is home all day, or one planning to electrify later and unsure of the load it will add.
  • Weak case: storage bought mainly as a backup generator. You can value resilience, but it will not always show up as a financial return.

Our savings estimator models both the solar-only and solar-plus-battery cases with your inputs, under the published assumptions. It will not tell you a battery is always better — because it is not — but it shows which numbers decide the answer for your household.

Key takeaways

  • kWh is storage capacity; kW is output power. A battery is fine at one and limited by the other.
  • Usable capacity and round-trip efficiency mean the delivered energy is less than the nameplate figure.
  • Value comes from the gap between what you pay for imports and what you are paid for exports.
  • Backup power depends on wiring and peak ratings — plan it deliberately.
  • Heat, cycling and placement shape lifespan as much as brand does.

Worth knowing

Blackout protection depends on the battery, inverter and the way the backup circuit is wired. Not every battery configuration can run your whole home during an outage — we will tell you exactly what yours will support.

What's included

  • Battery sizing based on your surplus and evening usage
  • Placement assessment for safety, clearance and ventilation requirements
  • Backup and blackout-protection capability explained honestly
  • Documentation for the installer's compliance and incentive paperwork
  • Monitoring setup so you can see charge, discharge and bill impact

Well suited to

  • Homes exporting a large share of solar at a low feed-in tariff
  • Households with meaningful evening and overnight usage
  • Anyone wanting some protection from outages

Common questions

Questions we are asked about this service

Short, direct answers. If your question is not here, ask it directly.

Compare both figures against what you need to run. Start by listing the evening loads you want covered and their combined power draw, then check the battery's continuous (kW) and usable (kWh) figures support them.

Usable capacity after depth-of-discharge limits, round-trip efficiency and the warranted throughput are the honest comparison points; nameplate capacity appearing in a brochure is not.

In most cases, yes. If your existing inverter is hybrid-capable, a DC-coupled battery may connect to it directly. Otherwise an AC-coupled battery with its own inverter runs alongside the existing system — the usual approach for retrofits.

The check-up points are inverter age and compatibility, switchboard capacity, wall space and clearances, backup circuit wishes, and whether the existing monitoring can report the battery.

Product warranties commonly run around ten years, and warranted throughput limits define how much energy the battery can cycle in that time. Realistic service life depends on usage patterns, placement and temperature — a well-placed, gently cycled battery typically fares best.

Ask for the warranty document, not just the warranty period: throughput limits, capacity guarantees and what happens at end of life are all defined there.

No — and it should not be expected to. Through winter and on heavy-cloud days there may be little surplus to store, while in summer the battery may fill by mid-morning. A battery is a long-term averaging tool, not a daily guarantee.

This is one reason savings estimates are presented as a range rather than a single figure. A battery that covers most of its modelled throughput across a year is performing as designed.

Sometimes. Air-conditioners draw a large starting surge, so both the battery's peak power rating and the inverter equipment determine whether it can start and run. A small split system on a dedicated backup circuit is often manageable; ducted systems across a whole house are a bigger ask.

If running specific appliances during an outage matters, name them during design so the backup circuit and equipment can be sized for those loads.
